# Recognition without a journal: how independent classics portals earned standing

**Bottom line.** Every independent resource below became "recognised" through the same five levers. None of them needed to be a journal:
1. Named, credentialed editors who take responsibility, and a visible review status on each item.
2. Precise, stable citation: standard reference schemes and permanent URLs, later numbered releases and DOIs.
3. Open licences and shared identifiers, so that other resources build on the work.
4. Evaluation by others: reviews of digital projects, conference papers and methods articles.
5. An institutional partner that hosts or funds the work but does not own the content.

For an AI-produced corpus, levers 1 and 4 matter most.

## 1. Case studies

- **Suda On Line** (1998–2014). Entries went live immediately but were marked "draft" until named editors vetted them to "low" or "high". Each entry shows its translator and every editor who revised it. Entries are cited by Adler numbers and stable URLs. Contributors listed their entries on their CVs. Over 200 contributors finished the translation on 21 July 2014. Sources: [history](https://www.cs.uky.edu/~raphael/sol/sol-html/history.shtml), [Mahoney, DHQ 3.1, 2009](https://dhq.digitalhumanities.org/vol/3/1/000025/000025.html).
- **Attic Inscriptions Online** (2012–). Led by an editor with an advisory board. It runs its own ISSN'd series, *AIO Papers* (ISSN 2054‑6777 online), where readings and translations are argued in detail ([AIO Papers](https://atticinscriptions.com/papers/aio-papers-10)). It is CC BY and EpiDoc. Funding came from the AHRC, Mellon and Humboldt, and the British School at Athens has managed it since 2021 ([wiki](https://wiki.digitalclassicist.org/Attic_Inscriptions_Online)). It was reviewed on the SCS blog and in *Classical Review*, which has reviewed digital projects since 2024 ([CUP blog](https://cambridge.org/core/blog/2025/04/09/digital-projects-reviews-the-importance-of-digital-resources-for-studying-and-teaching-the-ancient-world)).
- **EuripidesScholia.org** (Mastronarde). Published in numbered releases (1, 2, 3, then 3.1 in 2026), each announced through SCS news. Each release is also frozen as an eBook and PDF on Berkeley Pressbooks for preservation. A companion print monograph was reviewed in *CR* ([about](https://euripidesscholia.org/EurSch2025_About.html), [SCS](https://classicalstudies.org/scs-news/release-2-open-access-online-edition-scholia-orestes-euripides)).
- **Homer Multitext**. Hosted by the Center for Hellenic Studies. It published its editorial standards in DHQ and received an SCS review in 2018 ([DHQ](https://digitalhumanities.org/dhq/vol/3/1/000029/000029.html), [SCS](https://classicalstudies.org/scs-blog/bill-beck/review-reviewing-digital-edition-homer)).
- **Pleiades**. Built on "pervasive peer review" and CC BY. It has had NEH funding since 2006 and publishes numbered dataset releases with Zenodo DOIs, which it asks users to cite ([3.2](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.10070421)).
- **Trismegistos**. Its stable TM numbers became the field's shared identifier, and Wikidata has properties P1958, P8532, P11252 and others for it. It began with a Humboldt award in 2004 ([history](https://trismegistos.org/about_history.php)).
- **papyri.info**. Funded by Mellon and NEH. Its SoSOL editor sends contributions to an editorial board for review and keeps a version history ([about](https://papyri.info/docs/about)). Reviewed by SCS.
- **ToposText**. A one-person project (Kiesling) with a foundation sponsor (Laskaridis). Its texts carry CTS and Wikidata IDs, it links to Pleiades, and Wikidata has properties P8068–P8070 for its places, people and works ([wiki](https://wiki.digitalclassicist.org/ToposText)).
- **attalus.org, Livius.org and Roger Pearse**. One-person sites that gained standing through longevity, usefulness and openness. Attalus offers new translations, for example of Diodorus 33–40 ([attalus](https://attalus.org/info/diodorus.html)). Livius has run since 1996 and won awards; it hosted van der Spek's chronicles online before they appeared with SBL Press in 2025 ([Livius](https://livius.org/about), [SBL](https://cart.sbl-site.org/books/061560P)). Pearse puts his work in the public domain, now focuses on untranslated texts, and blogs about AI translation experiments ([post](https://www.roger-pearse.com/weblog/2023/07/26/is-it-a-waste-of-time-for-us-to-make-translations-of-ancient-texts/)).
- **Perseus/Scaife and Digital Loeb**. Scaife's CTS URNs make texts interoperable; the viewer was funded by a Humboldt chair ([OGL](https://opengreekandlatin.org/)). Digital Loeb has the publisher's brand and was still reviewed (Dik, *CJ* 110.4, 2015).
- **IOSPE³**. Hosted at King's College London in EpiDoc, with English translations by Polinskaya ([TEI](https://tei-c.org/activities/projects/ancient-inscriptions-of-the-northern-black-sea/)). I could not confirm the Russian partner or translations in this session: unknown.
- **AI translation projects**:
  - Sefaria's *Kli Yakar* is the first full English translation of that commentary. Claude 3.7 produced the draft, and a named specialist spent six months correcting it line by line ([Q&A](https://voices.sefaria.org/sheets/708436)). Sefaria marks AI content with icons that distinguish reviewed from unreviewed ([policy](https://www.sefaria.org/ai)).
  - Bibliothecarius Modernus offers 225 Latin patristic texts from the *Patrologia Latina* under CC0. It shows status labels such as unreviewed, spot-checked and human-reviewed, uses review by other AI model families, and calls its texts "introductory guides" ([GitHub](https://github.com/wryan14/Latin-Patristic-Texts)).
  - LITERA, a Latin translation system, published at NAACL Findings 2025 ([ACL](https://aclanthology.org/2025.findings-naacl.434/)).
  - Aeneas reached *Nature* (2025) with classicists as co-authors ([DeepMind](https://deepmind.google/discover/blog/aeneas-transforms-how-historians-connect-the-past/)).

## 2. Mechanisms, ranked for Neoscholia

1. **Editorial accountability.** A named board plus a visible status on each text. ISSN rules for websites require named editorial responsibility, "generally of more than one person", and exclude personal sites ([ISSN](https://www.issn.org/understanding-the-issn/assignment-rules/the-issn-for-electronic-media/)).
2. **Citation infrastructure.** Permanent URLs, standard section numbering, CTS URNs, numbered versions, Zenodo DOIs and ORCID. Crossref membership is open only to organisations; the lowest fee tier was US$200 a year from 2026, plus $1 per article ([fees](https://www.crossref.org/fees/)).
3. **Shared identifiers.** TEI XML and links to Pleiades, ToposText, Trismegistos and Wikidata. A Wikidata property for Neoscholia's own IDs has precedents in ToposText and the Patristic Text Archive (P13312–P13313).
4. **Listings.** AWOL ([AWOL](https://maryjahariscenter.org/resources/awol-the-ancient-world-online)), the Digital Classicist Wiki (accounts via its admins), the Stoa blog and the Digital Classicist mailing list ([Stoa](https://blog.stoa.org/about)).
5. **Reviews of digital projects.**
   - SCS Digital Project Reviews, running since 2016 with their own board ([SCS](https://classicalstudies.org/scs-news/scs-digital-project-reviews)).
   - *Classical Review*.
   - RIDE, which uses the [IDE criteria v1.1](https://www.i-d-e.de/publikationen/weitereschriften/criteria-version-1-1/) and separate text-collection criteria.
   - *Reviews in DH*: send a 500-word overview ([info](https://liberalarts.indianapolis.iu.edu/blogs/the-slate/new-journal-reviews-in-digital-humanities)).
   - BMCR tried electronic reviews but did not keep it up, so don't rely on it.
6. **Google Scholar.** It indexes scholarly-article forms only: one paper per URL, `citation_*` meta tags, PDFs under 5 MB ([guidelines](https://scholar.google.com/intl/en/scholar/inclusion.html)). Package translations as PDFs with an introduction.
7. **Standards to cite in self-documentation.** The IDE criteria, MLA CSE guidelines (CSE also awards a seal to qualifying digital editions; [CSE](https://scholarlyeditions.mla.hcommons.org/)) and [FAIR](https://www.nature.com/articles/sdata201618).
8. **Conferences.**
   - Digital Classicist London: the 2026 abstract deadline was 16 March, talks are streamed ([CFP](https://blog.stoa.org/archives/4370)).
   - DH2027 in Galway, 28 June–3 July 2027 ([ADHO](https://adho.org/conference/)).
   - AI-and-antiquity events such as the [Rouen study day (2026)](https://www.ecrituresnumeriques.ca/en/events/2026/02/06/study-day-antiquity-ai).

## 3. Credibility specific to AI translation

- **The evidence cuts against the niche.** The Galen study (Zainaldin et al., Feb 2026) scored LLM translations 95.2/100 on texts that already had translations but 79.9 on an untranslated one. Failures tracked rare terminology very closely (r = −0.97) ([arXiv](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.24119)). "First-ever" translations are exactly where LLMs are weakest. Human checking should therefore target passages dense in rare terms, and each text should carry a published quality sample.
- **Model reviews are quality control, not peer review.** Multi-model review is useful, but recognition needs named human reviewers. The precedents are Sefaria's six-month expert pass and Suda On Line's named vetting.
- **Disclose everything on each text.** Show the model and version, dates, which passages a human verified, and the reviewers' names. The AI is never listed as an author. COPE takes this stance, but its page could not be reached during this check.
- **No society policy found.** I found no SCS policy on AI translation; the field is experimenting (an SCS 2025 panel on AI in philology, [Dickinson](https://blogs.dickinson.edu/dcc/2025/01/07/scs-2025-panel-on-using-ai-in-classical-philology/embed/)).

## 4. Russian context

- **РИНЦ** indexes journals and non-periodicals (monographs, collections, conference materials) once their metadata is placed in eLIBRARY. I found no route for a website itself: **unknown**. Practical routes:
  - an annual ISBN'd collection, *Neoscholia. Труды*, placed in eLIBRARY;
  - articles in РИНЦ and Scopus journals. ΣΧΟΛΗ is in Scopus, WoS, РИНЦ, ERIH+ and DOAJ, CC BY ([ΣΧΟΛΗ](https://classics.nsu.ru/schole/)). ВДИ is peer-reviewed and in ERIH PLUS.
- **ISSN.** The Russian ISSN centre sits at the Russian State Library / Russian Book Chamber ([ISSN RF](https://www.issn.org/ru/centre/russian-federation-federation-de-russie)). An ISSN comes from the centre in the publisher's country.
- **Precedent and partner.** ancientrome.ru publishes "переводы, выполненные для сайта" (translations made for the site) and appears in the AWOL Index. It is a natural partner and place to announce.
- **Channels.**
  - Telegram: @sictransit (Sonkin) and @parakharatteintonomisma (Naranovich) ([mel.fm](https://mel.fm/prosveshcheniye/2309584-ancient_telegram)).
  - Сергеевские чтения at Moscow State University: every two years; the last was in January 2025, so the next is likely in 2027.
  - The Тронский readings at ИЛИ РАН in June (held 2021 and 2023).
  - Жебелевские чтения at St Petersburg State University (no dates found).
- **РНФ (Russian Science Foundation).** Grants go through Russian organisations. Eligibility of an independent researcher based abroad: unknown, requires a host institution.

## 5. Funding reality

- NEH: individuals and foreign entities are not eligible ([FAQ](https://www.neh.gov/sites/default/files/inline-files/DHAG%20FAQs%202023.pdf)).
- Loeb Classical Library Foundation: requires faculty status.
- **Gerda Henkel research scholarships**: no institutional affiliation needed; open to PhD holders of any nationality, for 1–24 months ([reflecta](https://foerdermittelkompass.reflecta.org/grants/allgemeine-foerderung-forschungsstipendien-gerda-henkel-stiftung?locale=en)). This is the best fit.
- ERC and Mellon fund through host institutions (not re-verified here).

## Unknowns

- Whether РИНЦ can index a website.
- The Russian side of IOSPE³.
- Who currently edits SCS digital reviews.
- Whether *Reviews in DH* is still taking submissions.
- How to submit to AWOL (the blog could not be fetched; contact Charles Jones).
- A real limit on research coverage: the session's web-search allowance (200 searches) ran out during this task. Russian DH channels and the Аристей journal could not be checked, so no claims are made about them.

roadmap.step: M0–2: Publish an Editorial Charter and AI-disclosure page. It sets out a status ladder per text (machine draft → editor-verified → externally reviewed by a named reviewer), records model, version and date for each text, lists which passages were human-verified, gives a corrections policy, and states licensing (CC BY 4.0 for translations and commentary). AI is never listed as an author.
roadmap.why: Every recognised precedent made its review state visible: Suda On Line's draft/low/high with named vetters, Sefaria's two AI icons, Bibliothecarius Modernus' status labels. The IDE criteria and SCS reviewers look for documented methods first.

roadmap.step: M0–4: Recruit a named advisory board of 4–7 scholars: Russian and international, covering Greek/Latin philology, Byzantine/patristic studies and digital humanities. Credit them on the site, and name external reviewers on each text page.
roadmap.why: This is the AIO model (editor plus advisory board). ISSN rules require editorial responsibility generally of more than one person. Named human vetting is what made Suda On Line citable.

roadmap.step: M1–3: Build the citation infrastructure: permanent URLs, standard section/line numbering (CTS URNs where a canonical work ID exists), a 'Cite this' box giving version and date, a changelog, and numbered releases per text.
roadmap.why: Suda On Line was cited by Adler number plus stable URL. EuripidesScholia and Pleiades ask users to cite numbered releases, which makes citations reproducible.

roadmap.step: M1–4: Keep TEI XML sources in a public Git repository. Publish each text release to Zenodo, which issues a DOI per version, inside a Neoscholia Zenodo community. Link ORCID iDs for the editor and reviewers.
roadmap.why: DOIs and versioned deposits are how Pleiades makes its data citable. They are free, and they connect the work to ORCID and library discovery systems.
roadmap.effort: About 1 week to set up, then about 2 h per release

roadmap.step: M2–4: Link the texts to shared identifiers: Pleiades, ToposText and Trismegistos IDs for places and people, Wikidata items for works and authors. Plan a CTS/DTS API endpoint later.
roadmap.why: ToposText and Trismegistos became indispensable because others could join their data to their identifiers. Scaife and Open Greek & Latin rely on CTS.

roadmap.step: M2–6: Run a flagship pilot. Fully human-verify one or two texts and publish a measured quality sample: an MQM-style score on selected passages, with passages dense in rare terminology flagged and checked by hand.
roadmap.why: The Galen study found that LLM quality falls on untranslated texts and that failures track rare terminology (r = −0.97). Publishing measured quality turns AI from a liability into documented method.

roadmap.step: M3–6: Apply for an ISSN, either for the portal as a continuously updated website or for a 'Neoscholia Papers' series modelled on AIO Papers, at the national ISSN centre of the publisher's country.
roadmap.why: An ISSN creates a catalogue record in the ISSN Portal and libraries and marks the site as an editorial publication rather than a personal site.

roadmap.step: M3–6: Make articles and translation-with-introduction PDFs eligible for Google Scholar: one item per URL, Highwire citation_* meta tags, PDFs under 5 MB, crawlable list pages.
roadmap.why: Google Scholar indexes only material in scholarly-article form. This is how citations of Neoscholia texts become visible and countable.

roadmap.step: M4–6: Get listed and announce launch. Targets: AWOL (Charles Jones); a Digital Classicist Wiki page (account via its admins); the Stoa blog and Digital Classicist mailing list; the Dig-Ed-Cat catalogue; the Reviews in DH registry; ancientrome.ru; Russian Telegram channels (@sictransit, @parakharatteintonomisma).
roadmap.why: AWOL and the Digital Classicist Wiki are the field's standard discovery layer. Every case study (ToposText, AIO, Euripides scholia) has a page there.

roadmap.step: M6–9: Create or enrich Wikidata items for each translated work. Once there are dozens of texts, propose a 'Neoscholia work ID' property. Do not add self-citations to Wikipedia yourself; disclose any conflict of interest.
roadmap.why: ToposText (P8068–P8070), Trismegistos and the Patristic Text Archive (P13312–P13313) gained infrastructure status through Wikidata properties. Wikipedia citations follow on from that.
roadmap.effort: 1–2 days per batch, plus the proposal

roadmap.step: M6–12: Write a public self-assessment against the IDE criteria and the SCS review guidelines. Then request reviews from SCS Digital Project Reviews, the Classical Review digital-projects section, RIDE (text-collections criteria) and Reviews in Digital Humanities.
roadmap.why: Third-party reviews are the main way digital projects earn recognition. AIO, HMT and papyri.info were all reviewed this way, and CR has reviewed digital projects since 2024.
roadmap.effort: 1 week to prepare, then 3–12 months of waiting

roadmap.step: M6–12: Publish two peer-reviewed articles. (a) An English methods paper on the AI-assisted first-translation workflow and its quality metrics, in Digital Classics Online, DHQ or DSH. (b) A Russian article with a specimen translation and commentary in ΣΧΟΛΗ or ВДИ.
roadmap.why: Methods papers gave HMT and Suda On Line academic standing. A РИНЦ/Scopus-indexed Russian article puts Neoscholia into the Russian citation system without giving up the portal.

roadmap.step: M8–15: Present at conferences: Digital Classicist London 2027 (abstracts likely due around mid-March 2027, by analogy with 2026); DH2027 in Galway, 28 June–3 July 2027 (call probably around December 2026); Сергеевские чтения 2027 at MSU (biennial); the Тронский readings at ИЛИ РАН (June); AI-and-antiquity study days.
roadmap.why: Talks put the work in front of the field's gatekeepers and create citable abstracts. Suda On Line built credibility the same way.

roadmap.step: M9–15: Set up a non-profit legal vehicle (for example an association in the editor's country of residence) to hold the project. Then join Crossref directly or through a sponsor, and accept donations and grants. Neoscholia keeps sole ownership of the content.
roadmap.why: Crossref accepts only organisations (lowest tier US$200 a year from 2026, $1 per article). Funders and partners need a counterparty. AIO shows that institutional hosting can coexist with editorial independence.

roadmap.step: M9–18: Apply for a Gerda Henkel research scholarship (no affiliation needed, for PhD holders) to fund research articles based on Neoscholia texts. In parallel, seek a visiting or honorary affiliation or an agreement with a university, so the project can join institution-only funders (NEH, ERC, РНФ) as a partner.
roadmap.why: NEH excludes individuals and foreign entities, the Loeb Foundation requires faculty status, and РНФ works through Russian organisations. Gerda Henkel is the best fit for an independent PhD.

roadmap.step: M12–18: Publish an annual 'Neoscholia. Papers / Труды' volume with ISBN and DOIs (articles and selected verified translations with introductions), and place its metadata in eLIBRARY/РИНЦ.
roadmap.why: РИНЦ indexes collections and monographs; I found no route for indexing a website itself. AIO Papers shows that an ISSN'd series beside a portal works.

roadmap.step: M12–24: Run an open, signed peer-review programme. Invite named reviewers per text, publish their reviews with DOIs so they count for the reviewers' records, and keep a public corrections tracker.
roadmap.why: Suda On Line's named vetting and papyri.info's board review with version history are the proven models. They also give reviewers a reason to take part.

roadmap.step: M18–24: Publish an annual transparency report covering usage, Google Scholar/РИНЦ/Wikipedia citations, corrections, and statistics on how much humans changed the AI drafts.
roadmap.why: Measured accountability answers the main objection to AI translation. Sefaria reports how many AI items its staff reviewed.

roadmap.step: M18–24 (optional): Consult the MLA Committee on Scholarly Editions about a flagship TEI edition, with a view to its seal.
roadmap.why: An external seal for digital editions; inspection covers the TEI encoding, documentation and interface. A long shot but high prestige.

checked.claim: Gerda Henkel research scholarships: no institutional affiliation needed, open to PhD holders of any nationality for 1–24 months; this is the best fit for the editor.
checked.correction: The affiliation, nationality and duration points are right. The foundation's own page says: 'No institutional affiliation is necessary'; 'Support does not depend on the applicant's nationality or location'; 'min. one month and max. 24 months'. But it adds conditions that probably rule the editor out. (1) 'The PhD must have been awarded not more than ten years earlier.' This limit does not apply to holders of a habilitation or equivalent. (2) 'Only full-time scholarships are available', and concurrent employment or a pension is not allowed. (3) The dissertation must be published, and the project 'must differ clearly from the topic of the PhD thesis'. Rates are EUR 2,760 a month for postdocs and EUR 3,720 with a habilitation. The editor's PhD was followed by a long IT career, so the 10-year limit very likely excludes them. Gerda Henkel should not be called the 'best fit' without checking the PhD date. The reflecta listing's 'Germany' is the funder's location, not an applicant restriction.

checked.claim: Crossref membership is open only to organisations; the lowest fee tier is US$200 a year from 2026, plus $1 per article.
checked.correction: Only organisations can join: 'Membership in Crossref is open to organisations that produce professional and scholarly materials and content.' But the US$200 tier applies only where total publishing revenue or expenses are under US$1,000. From US$1,000 to US$1 million the fee is US$275, and above that it is US$550 or more. The fees page does not say when the $200 tier started, so 'from 2026' is unverified. Content registration (2026) costs $1.00 per current journal article, $0.25 per book chapter, $0.06 per dataset and $0.25 per peer review. Volume discounts ended on 1 Jan 2026, and most per-record prices fall from 1 Jan 2027. Alternative: more than half of members join through a Sponsor and pay Crossref no membership fee themselves (the sponsor may charge). For a non-profit with almost no budget, the $200 tier or a sponsor is realistic, but the roadmap should not quote $200 without the revenue condition.

checked.claim: ISSN rules for websites require named editorial responsibility 'generally of more than one person' and exclude personal sites; the ISSN comes from the centre in the publisher's country; the Russian centre is at the Russian State Library / Book Chamber.
checked.correction: Verbatim, an eligible site must 'present editorial content (written text), mention the editorial responsibility, comprised generally of more than one person (name of the editor or publisher)'. It must also have a stable title and URL and 'cover a precise subject or address a specific target audience'. Excluded are 'personal content: personal website, online personal diary', 'a short-lived resource' and sites 'focused on a company, product, institution or organisation'. The request form routes by country of publication; where there is no national centre, the International Centre handles it. The Russian centre is the 'ISSN National Centre of the Russian Federation' at the Russian State Library (Book Chamber, Zvezdny blvd 17, Moscow; rsl.ru/ru/rkp). Precedent: AIO Papers carries ISSN 2054-6769 (print) and 2054-6777 (online). It is published by 'Attic Inscriptions Online' at a UK postal address with a named editor (S. D. Lambert) and a six-member advisory board, not by a university press.

checked.claim: Zenodo issues a DOI per version; numbered releases with Zenodo DOIs are free and citable (Pleiades 3.2 as model).
checked.correction: Zenodo registers 'a DOI representing the specific version' plus a Concept DOI 'representing all of the versions'. The roadmap should cite the version DOI for static citations and the concept DOI for 'latest'. Policies: 50 GB per record (more on request); items are kept 'for the lifetime of the repository' (CERN); after withdrawal 'The DOI and the URL of the original object are retained' with a tombstone page; every public file needs a licence; metadata is CC0. The policies page fetched does not mention cost, so 'free' was not re-verified there. Pleiades Datasets 3.2 (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.10070421) dates from 3 Nov 2023, is CC BY 4.0 and says 'We encourage use and citation of these numbered releases'. Newer versions exist, so the report should cite the concept DOI rather than 3.2.

checked.claim: Google Scholar indexes only scholarly-article forms: one paper per URL, citation_* meta tags, PDFs under 5 MB. Package translations as PDFs with an introduction.
checked.correction: Verbatim: content 'must consist primarily of scholarly articles - journal papers, conference papers, technical reports, or their drafts, dissertations, pre-prints, post-prints, or abstracts'. News, magazine articles, book reviews and editorials are excluded. 'Each paper must have its own unique URL'. Highwire (citation_title), BE Press and PRISM tags are supported; citation_title, citation_author and citation_publication_date are required. 'Each file must not exceed 5MB in size'. Larger documents such as books should go to Google Book Search, which Scholar includes automatically. Translations are not mentioned at all. Packaging each text as an article-like item with an introduction is a reasonable inference, but indexing is not guaranteed.

checked.claim: RIDE reviews digital editions using the IDE criteria v1.1 and separate text-collection criteria; Neoscholia can request a RIDE review.
checked.correction: RIDE is 'an open access review journal dedicated to digital editions and resources'. It uses three catalogues: Criteria for Reviewing Scholarly Digital Editions v1.1, Criteria for Reviewing Digital Text Collections v1.0, and Criteria for Reviewing Tools and Environments for Digital Scholarly Editing v1.0. A separate 'FAIR Principles in Editions' handout is also used. A project cannot simply submit itself. Reviews are written by external reviewers who must 'contact the editor(s) ... before beginning to work on your review'. RIDE keeps a wish-list of projects but is 'happy to consider your suggestions'. So Neoscholia can suggest itself to the editors or find a reviewer; it cannot commission a review. A corpus of AI translations fits the text-collections catalogue best.

checked.claim: Galen study (Zainaldin et al., Feb 2026): LLM translations scored 95.2/100 on already-translated text vs 79.9 on an untranslated one; failures track rare terminology (r = −0.97).
checked.correction: arXiv 2602.24119 is by Zainaldin, Pattison, Marai, Wu and Schiefsky (submitted 27 Feb 2026, revised 15 Apr 2026). Quoted: 'mean MQM score 95.2/100' on the translated expository text and '79.9/100' on the untranslated pharmacological text; 'Terminology rarity ... emerged as the dominant predictor of failure (r = -.97)'. Caveat: the two texts differ in genre (expository vs pharmacological) as well as in whether a translation exists. The drop is therefore not purely an 'untranslated' effect. The paper's own explanation is terminology rarity, which strengthens the advice to aim human checking at passages dense in rare terms.

checked.claim: Classical Review has reviewed digital projects since 2024 and reviewed Attic Inscriptions Online.
checked.correction: The AIO review is confirmed: J. R. W. Prag, 'Attic Inscriptions Online', ed. S. Lambert, C. de Lisle, P. Low, P. Liddel, CR 75.1 (April 2025), pp. 63–65, doi:10.1017/s0009840x25000848. The 2024 evidence is narrower than claimed. CR 74.1 (online 29 Jan 2024), pp. 1–19, opened with a survey article by Barker, Palladino and Gordin, 'Digital Approaches to Investigating Space and Place in Classical Studies'. No single-project review from 2024 was found in Crossref. The CUP blog post (April 2025) that would date the section returned HTTP 403. Wording should be: 'CR has run digital-project reviews since at least 2025 (AIO, CR 75.1), preceded by a 2024 survey article.' How to propose a project to CR: unknown.

checked.claim: NEH: individuals and foreign entities are not eligible.
checked.correction: Foreign entities: confirmed. FAQ Q5: 'NEH does not provide financial assistance to foreign institutions or organizations.' Q6: eligible U.S. institutions may engage foreign individuals only 'as consultants ... on a fee-for-service basis'. Q7: project directors need not be U.S. citizens if the applicant institution is eligible. The fetched FAQ (marked 'Updated: August 16, 2022', despite '2023' in the file name) does not itself state the exclusion of individuals; that is in the NOFO, which was not fetched. The practical conclusion stands: NEH is reachable only through a U.S. institutional partner.

checked.claim: EuripidesScholia.org is published in numbered releases (1, 2, 3, then 3.1 in 2026), each frozen as eBook and PDF on Berkeley Pressbooks.
checked.correction: This is out of date. The site now shows 'Release 4 (officially released September 27, 2026)', and further portions are projected for 2028 and 2030. Earlier releases are archived as eBooks on Berkeley Pressbooks and as PDFs on eScholarship: Release 1 (escholarship.org/uc/item/7xp733bb), Release 2 (archived Feb 2024, item/8s30w6g5) and Release 3/3.1 (archived Feb 2026, item/4d77s039). The PDFs are on eScholarship, not Pressbooks. The report's About URL (EurSch2025_About.html) now returns 404; the current page is EurSch2026_About.html. Funding is acknowledged from Mastronarde's Melpomene Chair fund, with hosting by the UC Berkeley Library.

checked.claim: Attic Inscriptions Online: led by an editor with an advisory board; CC BY, EpiDoc; funded by AHRC, Mellon, Humboldt; managed by the British School at Athens since 2021; reviewed on the SCS blog.
checked.correction: Mostly confirmed. AIO /about lists Humboldt, Mellon and AHRC (AH/P015069/1) among its funders, and says 'In February 2021 overall responsibility for the site was transferred to the British School at Athens'. The leadership has changed. Academic content is now overseen by 'an Editorial Committee consisting of Chris de Lisle, Polly Low, and Peter Liddel', plus an advisory board; Lambert was sole editor in AIO Papers 10 (2019/2020). CC BY and EpiDoc are per the Digital Classicist wiki, not stated on AIO's own about page. The AIO Papers PDF is marked 'All rights reserved', so CC BY does not cover the Papers series. The SCS review is A. Sheppard, SCS Digital Reviews (2017), per the wiki.

checked.claim: AI-translation precedents: Sefaria's Kli Yakar (Claude 3.7 draft, six-month expert edit, first full English translation, two AI icons); Bibliothecarius Modernus (225 PL texts, CC0, status labels, cross-model review, 'introductory guides').
checked.correction: Sefaria describes 'the first-ever complete English translation of the Kli Yakar Torah commentary'. Claude 3.7 produced the draft, and Rav Francis Nataf edited for 'six months', comparing 'every word to the original Hebrew'. Icons: an outlined star marks AI-assisted content that has had human review; a filled star marks fully AI-generated content without review. The policy page gives no count of reviewed AI items beyond about 1,000 reviewed Topic pages, so the roadmap's 'Sefaria reports how many AI items its staff reviewed' is only weakly supported. Bibliothecarius Modernus: 225 works from Migne's PL, CC0 1.0, labels coverage-verified / human-reviewed / spot-checked / defect-recorded / unreviewed, 'an independent review by a model of a different family', and to be treated as 'introductory guides rather than scholarly editions'.

checked.claim: Suda On Line: entries marked draft until vetted; completed 21 July 2014 by over 200 contributors; contributors listed entries on CVs. Wikidata has ToposText P8068–P8070, Patristic Text Archive P13312–P13313, Trismegistos P1958/P8532/P11252.
checked.correction: SOL history: the last entry was submitted on 21 July 2014 and 'vetted the next day'; there were 'over 200 individuals from five continents and more than 20 countries'; entries are 'marked clearly as draft until vetted'; contributions 'can be listed as published scholarly works on the students' CV's'. The draft/low/high ladder is not on the history page; per the report it comes from Mahoney's DHQ article, which was not re-fetched. Wikidata labels confirmed: P8068/P8069/P8070 are ToposText place/person/work IDs; P13312/P13313 are Patristic Text Archive author/work IDs; P1958 is Trismegistos Geo ID, P8532 Trismegistos text ID and P11252 Trismegistos author ID.

checked.claim: Venues: ΣΧΟΛΗ is in Scopus, WoS, РИНЦ, ERIH+, DOAJ, CC BY; Digital Classicist London 2026 abstracts due 16 March, streamed; DH2027 Galway 28 June–3 July 2027.
checked.correction: ΣΧΟΛΗ lists Scopus, Web of Science, РИНЦ, CEEOL, DOAJ and ERIH Plus, under CC BY. Digital Classicist London 2026: 300-word abstracts 'by the end of Monday 16th March 2026' to gabriel.bodard@sas.ac.uk; seminars are 'simultaneously streamed ... on Youtube'. ADHO: DH2027 at the University of Galway, 28 June–3 July 2027. DH2026 was in Daejeon (27 July–1 Aug 2026) with submissions due 15 December 2025, which supports the roadmap's guess of a DH2027 call around December 2026; the DH2027 deadline itself is not yet posted.

checked.claim: SCS Digital Project Reviews have run since 2016 with their own board; the MLA CSE awards a seal to qualifying digital editions.
checked.correction: classicalstudies.org returned HTTP 403 for all URLs tried, and scholarlyeditions.mla.hcommons.org also returned 403, so neither claim could be re-checked. Indirect evidence: the Digital Classicist wiki lists an SCS Digital Review of AIO by A. Sheppard (2017), which fits a series active by 2017. The start date of 2016, the current editors and the CSE seal procedure remain unknown.

verify.summary:
I re-checked 15 groups of decision-critical claims. All were checked by fetching primary pages directly, because the session's web-search allowance (200 searches) was already used up. 8 were confirmed (some with caveats), 6 need correction and 1 could not be checked.

**Biggest correction: Gerda Henkel is probably not available to the editor.** The foundation's own page requires the PhD to be no more than 10 years old (unless the applicant has a habilitation), and allows only full-time scholarships with no other job or pension. The project must also differ clearly from the thesis topic. The roadmap's "best fit" recommendation should be dropped or made conditional on the PhD date.

**Other corrections:**
- **Crossref:** the US$200 tier applies only to organisations with under US$1,000 in publishing revenue or expenses. From $1,000 to $1 million the fee is $275. "From 2026" is not stated on the fees page. Registration costs $1 per journal article, $0.25 per book chapter and $0.06 per dataset, with prices falling in 2027. Joining through a Sponsor is a fee-free alternative, and individuals cannot join.
- **Classical Review:** its AIO review is confirmed (Prag, CR 75.1, 2025). "Digital-project reviews since 2024" rests only on a 2024 survey article by Barker, Palladino and Gordin.
- **EuripidesScholia:** now at Release 4 (27 Sep 2026). The PDFs are on eScholarship and the eBooks on Berkeley Pressbooks. The report's About link is dead.
- **AIO:** an Editorial Committee now runs it (de Lisle, Low, Liddel), and the British School at Athens has been responsible since Feb 2021. The AIO Papers PDF is "All rights reserved", not CC BY.
- **Sefaria:** the claim that it reports counts of reviewed AI items is only weakly supported.

**Confirmed:**
- **ISSN rules for websites:** "generally of more than one person"; personal and short-lived sites are excluded; the centre is chosen by country of publication. The Russian centre is at the Russian State Library. AIO Papers (ISSN 2054-6777) is a precedent for a series published by a project rather than a press.
- **Zenodo:** one DOI per version plus a concept DOI; 50 GB per record; DOI kept after withdrawal. Cost was not stated on the policies page.
- **Google Scholar:** article-type content only, one paper per URL, citation_* tags, files under 5 MB. Translations are not mentioned.
- **RIDE:** three criteria sets (editions v1.1, text collections v1.0, tools v1.0) plus a FAIR handout. Reviewers must contact the editors first, and projects can only suggest themselves.
- **Galen study:** 95.2 vs 79.9 and r = −.97 confirmed. Caveat: the two texts also differ in genre, so the drop is not purely an "untranslated" effect.
- **NEH:** foreign institutions are excluded. The exclusion of individuals is in the funding notice, not the FAQ.
- **Also confirmed:** the Sefaria Kli Yakar and Bibliothecarius Modernus details, Suda On Line's completion date and contributor count, the Wikidata property IDs, ΣΧΟΛΗ's indexing, the Digital Classicist London 2026 deadline, and DH2027 in Galway.

**Not checked:** SCS Digital Project Reviews (start date and editors) and the MLA CSE seal. Both sites returned HTTP 403.
